candidate.title: STEM Design: compare two flashlight switches

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Explain how a complete conducting path and an open switch affect a compatible battery and lamp circuit.
Without the worked example, explain: Plan a fair comparison of two contact designs, record honestly attributed observations and explain a controlled revision.

pedagogy.rationale: Explain the circuit, plan two designs, observe honestly, revise one contact feature and make a numerical comparison. Reasoning and evidence are assessed; physical success is not a grade.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Count whole numbers from zero to five and compare two counts.
Use labelled sketches and explain an idea orally or with a scribe.

misconceptions.description: The switch creates the energy that lights the lamp.
misconceptions.response: The battery supplies energy. Closing the switch completes a conducting path; the switch does not create energy.

misconceptions.description: One successful test proves the switch always works.
misconceptions.response: Record every trial, including failures. Five trials support a limited comparison, not a guarantee.

misconceptions.description: Changing several components establishes which single change caused an outcome.
misconceptions.response: Change one contact feature while keeping battery, bulb, wires and procedure fixed.

misconceptions.description: The taller closed-switch bar proves the best design without checking open-switch control.
misconceptions.response: Use both closed-light and open-dark observations, and acknowledge the limits of the tests.

scenes.title: A light we can control
scenes.learnerAction: Sketch a complete path and explain how opening the switch changes it.

content.body: Our design challenge is a small flashlight switch. The battery, compatible lamp and conducting wires must form a complete path for the lamp to light. An open switch breaks that path. The battery supplies energy; the switch controls the connection. Engineering Design here is a LiberiaLearn STEM activity, not an official Ministry subject claim.

prompts.prompt: Draw or describe where the path is broken when the switch is open.

scenes.title: Understand the circuit and the limits
scenes.learnerAction: Explain the source of energy and why every trial matters.

content.body: Use only a teacher-checked, enclosed low-voltage kit. Never use mains electricity or loose button cells. Do not short the battery. Stop if parts warm; adults handle cutting. A design should light on at least four of five closures and stay dark on all five openings. These are design criteria, not your grade.

hints: Trace the path from one battery terminal through the lamp and back.
Separate a recorded result from a prediction about a future test.

accessibility.textAlternative: Use only a teacher-checked, enclosed low-voltage kit. Never use mains electricity or loose button cells. Do not short the battery. Stop if parts warm; adults handle cutting. A design should light on at least four of five closures and stay dark on all five openings. These are design criteria, not your grade. Why can closing the switch light a working circuit? Options: The lamp gets its energy from the switch instead of the battery.; It completes the path so energy from the battery can be transferred.; The switch makes new energy each time it closes.. What can one successful closure establish? Options: The lamp lit on that trial; we still need the other observations.; It proves every future closure will work.; One success can stand for all five trials without testing them..

scenes.title: Plan before changing the contacts
scenes.learnerAction: State what changes, what stays fixed and why the comparison is useful.

content.body: Sketch two contact arrangements. Predict how changing one contact feature could affect the light. Keep the same battery, lamp, wires and procedure. Work in groups of three to five with rotating jobs: planner, supervised builder, observer, recorder and evidence-checker. Combine jobs in smaller groups. Everyone should explain a decision.

prompts.prompt: Describe both contact arrangements. Identify one changed feature and the controls.
Predict an effect and explain why it might occur.

hints: Change a contact feature, not several components at once.
Your prediction needs a reason that could be checked.

items.prompt: Which plan lets us compare one contact change fairly?

options.text: Widen one contact. Keep the same battery, lamp, wires and procedure.
options.feedback: One contact feature changes. The other parts and procedure stay fixed, so the comparison investigates that change.

options.text: Widen one contact and use a brighter lamp for Design 2.
options.feedback: Both the contact and the lamp change. You could not tell which change affected the result. Keep the lamp fixed.

options.text: Change the contact, battery and wires together for Design 2.
options.feedback: Several parts change together. A different result would not identify the effect of the contact. Change one feature and keep the kit fixed.

scenes.title: Test, compare and draw your graph
scenes.learnerAction: Complete both available observation records, source labels and the hand-drawn graph before leaving this activity.

content.body: Keep this activity open while completing both designs. Record five closed and five open observations for each design. Record all outcomes honestly. After Design 1, state one contact change and why its evidence suggests that change; then test Design 2. On paper copy both rows, draw two labelled bars from the closed-light counts with a zero baseline and scale to five, and check the open-dark counts too.

answerGuidance.circuit: A closed conducting path connects the battery and compatible lamp; opening the switch breaks the path. The switch does not create energy.
answerGuidance.fairTest: Change one contact feature; keep battery, lamp, wires and procedure fixed. Distinguish an observation from a prediction. Record all actual outcomes, including failures.
answerGuidance.designComparison: Use all five closed and five open trials per design. Accept unchanged or worse second-design results when interpreted honestly. Five trials do not prove unlimited reliability.
answerGuidance.graph: Paper bars are labelled Design 1 and Design 2, with closed-light successes out of five, baseline zero and scale to five. Inspect open-dark counts separately before recommending.
answerGuidance.provenance: Physical/group observations are MEASURED. Approved provided observations are SUPPLIED, not the learner's own tests. No dataset is present. SIMULATED remains unavailable pending scientific/model approval.
answerGuidance.access: Without observed group trials or reviewed provided data, sketches and test plans are partial work. Never enter invented counts, zeros or a false claim of completed physical testing.

teacherGuide.classification: Grade 4 applied STEM learning component. Primary standard: Engineering Design. Formal classification is provisional until standards mapping is completed. No official Ministry subject claim.
teacherGuide.paperReasoning: Sketch and explain the complete/open circuit. From Design 1 observations, propose one controlled change before seeing Design 2 observations. Analyze both rows, draw the graph, justify a choice and identify a further test.
teacherGuide.providedData: Use a separate MEASUREMENT_TABLE with origin ILLUSTRATIVE and originNote: Provided by the lesson. These are not your measurements. Label SUPPLIED and record empirical adult/teacher source (who, when, kit) or constructed status, protocol and dataset hash. CoS independently reviews the dataset before use. No dataset is supplied by this input revision.
teacherGuide.virtualData: Only CoS-approved scientific model/version and contract-permitted use. Label SIMULATED in scene text and originNote, identify model limits, and never call it physical contact-reliability evidence. Provided virtual results follow the separately reviewed SUPPLIED dataset route.
teacherGuide.routeHonesty: Use the completion label analysed provided observations for the provided-data route; do not mark tested two designs fulfilled. A group observer says observed my group's test, not I built and measured. Both routes use the same reasoning rubric without penalizing access to equipment.
teacherGuide.noEvidence: If neither reviewed data nor observed group trials are available, offer sketch and test-plan only. Keep counts missing and the comparison incomplete; never invent counts or substitute zero.
teacherGuide.sharedKits: Use 3–5 learners per teacher-checked kit; rotate planner/explainer, supervised builder, observer/counter, recorder and evidence-checker. Combine roles for smaller groups and obtain each learner's reasoning. Adults make safety decisions.
teacherGuide.assessment: Reasoning-only formative evidence; no official grades, records or persistent mastery. Separate governed assessment remains a release dependency.
teacherGuide.safety: Teacher checks enclosed low-voltage batteries and a compatible bulb. No mains, loose button cells, damaged cells, direct shorts or hot wires. Stop if parts warm. Adults handle cutting and real safety decisions.
teacherGuide.fairTest: Change one contact feature while holding battery, bulb, wires and test procedure fixed. State what you changed, why the first results motivated it and how the second test informs the decision.
teacherGuide.continuousActivity: DESIGN_CYCLE and linked MEASUREMENT_TABLE remain in the same scene and ActivityScope for both attempts. Copy observations/source labels to paper before leaving. The graph is drawn on paper, not a GRAPH_BUILDER block.
teacherGuide.recording: Use one row per design and track every closed/open trial separately on paper before recording counts. Record integers 0–5, with missing counts left missing. The design identifiers are fixed row headers, never measurements.

graphTask.instructions: Draw two bars on paper or squared paper: Design 1 and Design 2 across the bottom; successful closed-switch trials from 0 to 5 up the side. Copy each height from the matching row, then compare both open-switch counts in the table before choosing.
responseFields: CALCULATED difference between the two counts
INFERRED comparison and choice, checking open-switch counts too
graphTask.teacherCheck: Check both bar heights and fixed labels against the selected source table, a zero baseline and scale to 5. A missing observation is not zero; the comparison stays incomplete.
graphTask.provenance: Label the graph MEASURED when based on actual learner/group observations; SUPPLIED when using reviewed provided data; SIMULATED when based on approved model trials. Graphing does not change the source class.

teacherGuide.review: Check both attempts, the changed contact feature, controls, both table rows, graph heights, open-dark results and justified choice. Read the pupil's individual explanation, not merely a group answer.
teacherGuide.secondDesignFeedback: Judge Design 2 on its own results; compare with Design 1. Do not presume that a revision improves performance. Do not grade equipment performance.

completionLabels.noData: sketch and test-plan only; comparison incomplete

teacherGuide.providedDataStatus: NONE_INCLUDED. Separate dataset/source/hash review and separately labelled ILLUSTRATIVE table required before use. Do not auto-fill the learner-measured table.
teacherGuide.simulatedRoute: UNAVAILABLE until circuit-lab scientific validation and CoS model-version approval.
teacherGuide.duration: 45 minutes is a proposed allocation, not a measured classroom rehearsal. Use shared kits and teacher-managed turns; do not rush safety or fabricate missing results.
teacherGuide.retention: After seven days retrieve the complete/open-path explanation and propose a controlled comparison without reopening worked support. No scheduler is activated.

learnerPaperRecord.instructions: Use these labels on your paper record. Record only available observations. Row 1 is Design 1; Row 2 is Design 2. Keep both original rows and your graph.
learnerPaperRecord.evidence: counted (MEASURED): actual counts you observed or your group observed; name the observer/group. given to us (SUPPLIED): independently reviewed provided observations; identify the source. Never call supplied observations your own measurements.
learnerPaperRecord.design1: Source label and reference: ____ . Closed-light successes out of five: ____ . Open-dark successes out of five: ____ .
learnerPaperRecord.revision: Contact feature changed: ____ . My reason from Design 1 observations: ____ . Kit and procedure kept fixed: ____ .
learnerPaperRecord.design2: Source label and reference: ____ . Closed-light successes out of five: ____ . Open-dark successes out of five: ____ .
learnerPaperRecord.graph: Draw the two bars from the closed-light counts. Label Design 1 and Design 2. Start the scale at zero and end at five. Check the open-dark counts before choosing.
learnerPaperRecord.calculation: worked out (CALCULATED): difference between the two bar heights: ____ . Show how you worked it out.
learnerPaperRecord.inference: my conclusion (INFERRED): my choice or next change: ____ . Numerical reason using both designs and both criteria: ____ . Limitation or further test: ____ .

STEM Design: compare two flashlight switches

A light we can control

Our design challenge is a small flashlight switch. The battery, compatible lamp and conducting wires must form a complete path for the lamp to light. An open switch breaks that path. The battery supplies energy; the switch controls the connection. Engineering Design here is a LiberiaLearn STEM activity, not an official Ministry subject claim. Understand the circuit and the limits

Use only a teacher-checked, enclosed low-voltage kit. Never use mains electricity or loose button cells. Do not short the battery. Stop if parts warm; adults handle cutting. A design should light on at least four of five closures and stay dark on all five openings. These are design criteria, not your grade. Why can closing the switch light a working circuit? Options: The lamp gets its energy from the switch instead of the battery.; It completes the path so energy from the battery can be transferred.; The switch makes new energy each time it closes..
